title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, give your name, ask how someone is, and know when to say *u* and when *je* is enough.
bekal: greet people from morning to night with the right greeting
introduce yourself and ask other people's names
choose between *je* (casual) and *u* (polite) without a misstep

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Op de taalschool
dialogs.intro: First day of a language course in Amsterdam. Budi sits down next to someone he doesn't know yet.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Hello Sanne. My name is Budi.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. How are you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Goed, dank je. En met jou?
lines.literal: good, thank you. and with you?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Ook goed. Ben jij nieuw hier?
lines.id: Fine too. Are you new here?
lines.literal: also good. are you new here?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, het is mijn eerste dag.
lines.literal: yes, it is my first day.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Leuk! Sorry, hoe heet je ook alweer?
lines.id: Nice! Sorry, what was your name again?
lines.literal: nice! sorry, how are-called you also again?

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: Goedemorgen allemaal. Hoe gaat het met u, meneer?
lines.id: Good morning, everyone. How are you, sir?
lines.literal: good-morning all. how goes it with you, sir?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Very well, thank you very much.

notes: **Ik heet Budi** literally means "I am called Budi" — *heten* is a verb, not a noun. Dutch doesn't say "my name is" as its everyday phrase; it says "I am called". Another correct option is *Mijn naam is Budi*, but it sounds formal, like introducing yourself on an office phone.
**Ik ben Sanne** and **Ik heet Sanne** are both used and both correct. *Ik ben* is a little more relaxed.
**Hoe gaat het?** literally means "how goes it?" — not "how are you?". So the answer is about "it" too, not about "I": *Het gaat goed* (it goes well). In quick conversation, people just say *Goed!*

**Dank je** is for people you call *je*; **dank u** for people you call *u*. Adding *wel* makes it warmer: *dank je wel*, *dank u wel*. Mixing them up sounds like saying "cheers, mate" to a university president.
**En met jou?** — "and with you?" Note *jou*, not *je*: after a preposition (*met*, *voor*, *van*) the full form is used. The polite version: *En met u?*
**Hoe heet je ook alweer?** is a ready-made phrase for "what was your name again?" — it rescues a lot of conversations. Its literal meaning makes no sense ("also again"), so learn it as a whole.
**Tot straks** = see you later (the same day). The family is big: *tot ziens* (goodbye, neutral), *tot morgen* (see you tomorrow), *tot zo* (see you in a bit), *doei* (bye, very casual).

grammars.title: Zijn — the most important verb in Dutch
body: Just like English "I am a teacher", Dutch *cannot* drop the verb: *ik ben leraar*. The verb *zijn* (to be) must be there, and it is the only Dutch verb whose forms are truly all over the place — learn it like a song. Note that Dutch leaves out the article with jobs: *ik ben leraar*, not "a teacher".
after: Note that *zij* means both **she** and **they** — only the verb form tells them apart: *zij is* (she) versus *zij zijn* (they).
Each pronoun has a full form and a weak form: *jij/je*, *wij/we*, *zij/ze*, *mij/me*. The weak form is the everyday one; the full form is for emphasis — *Ik ben moe, maar jíj bent nog wakker*.

grammars.title: Je or u? The Dutch rules of politeness
body: The Netherlands is famous for its flat hierarchy, and you can hear it in the language: *je* is used far more widely than most learners expect.
after: When in doubt, start with *u*. The Dutch will quickly cut in with *Zeg maar je* ("just call me je") — and after that, going back to *u* actually feels cold.
⚠️ Don't mix *u* and *jij* in one sentence. *Hoe heet u?* or *Hoe heet je?* — never *Hoe heet u, jij?*

blocks.text: *Dag* is the most versatile word in Dutch: it means "day" (the same word as English *day*), it is used to say hello, and it is used to say goodbye. Said twice with a rising-falling tune (*dag-dag!*), it becomes a warm, typically Dutch farewell.

blocks.title: Saying goodbye
items: *Tot ziens* (tot ZEENS) — goodbye, neutral and safe with anyone.
*Doei* / *doeg* (dooy) — bye, casual, only for people you call *je*.
*Tot morgen* / *tot straks* / *tot zo* — see you tomorrow / see you later / see you in a bit.
*Fijne dag!* (FEY-nuh dakh) — have a nice day. The reply: *Jij ook!*

English
rows: What is your name? (formal, at a counter)

blocks.text: *Ik versta je niet* and *ik begrijp het niet* are different: the first means you didn't catch the sounds, the second means you don't understand the meaning. In your first weeks you will need the first one more often.
The letter names you'll use most when spelling

Non-Dutch names almost always need spelling out in the Netherlands. The usual troublemakers: **y** (the Dutch hear it as *ij*), **c** (said "say"), **j** (said "yay" — the Dutch *j* is an English *y*) and **u** (said "ü", not "oo" — if your name has a u, say *u zoals in Utrecht*).

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of zijn (ben, bent, is, zijn).
Choose the right greeting for the time of day.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: ben — bent — is — zijn — zijn — bent
Ik heet Budi. — Hoe gaat het? — Goed, dank je. — Hoe heet u? — Ik ben nieuw hier. — Tot morgen!
Ik heet Budi. — Hoe heet je? — Het is mijn eerste dag. — Hoe gaat het met u? — Dank je wel.
